title: Percent in the shop's mirror
summary: Turn the ledger's numbers into percents, so a stand and a supermarket can be judged on the same scale, and name what a yes costs. Then three geometry peaks: angles that must add up, areas chopped into easy pieces, and right triangles you can spot by their sides.
materials: your closing numbers from the stand: takings, every cost, and the hours you put in
a calculator, allowed only after the sum is written down

problems.prompt: A weather sensor takes a reading every 15 seconds, day and night. About how many readings does it take in one day?
explanation: Climb one hop at a time: 60 seconds divided by 15 seconds is 4 readings a minute.
4 readings a minute times 60 minutes is 240 readings an hour.
240 readings an hour times 24 hours is 5,760 readings, which rounds to about 6,000.
problems.useAgain: when a rate has to climb second to minute to hour to a whole day, and only the size of the answer matters.
hints: Work out how many readings happen in one minute first, before you touch the hours.
Climb the hops in order: second to minute, minute to hour, hour to the whole day.
problems.socraticHint: If the sensor read every 30 seconds instead of every 15, would today's answer double or halve?

variant.prompt: A weather sensor takes a reading every 20 seconds, day and night. About how many readings does it take in one day?

problems.prompt: A supermarket keeps about 2 dollars of profit out of every 100 dollars of shopping it sells. Suppose one store takes 40,000 dollars in a day. About how much profit does it keep from that day?
explanation: Find one hundredth of the takings first: 40,000 shared into 100 lots is 400 dollars a lot.
The store keeps 2 of those lots, and 2 lots of 400 is 800 dollars.
A thin slice still makes real money, because the slice is taken 400 times over in one day.
problems.useAgain: when a slice per hundred has to be sized against a takings number too big to picture.
hints: How many hundreds are there inside 40,000?
Work out one hundredth of the takings; the 2 can wait until you have it.
problems.socraticHint: Does a thin slice always mean small money, or does something else in this question decide that?

variant.prompt: A corner shop keeps about 5 dollars of profit out of every 100 dollars it sells, and takes 2,000 dollars in a day. About how much profit is that?

problems.prompt: Suppose you leave 40 dollars in an account that pays about 3 dollars a year for every 100 dollars in it. About how much does the account pay you in one year?
explanation: 3 dollars for every 100 is 3 cents for every dollar.
40 dollars collecting 3 cents each is 120 cents.
120 cents is a dollar and 20 cents, so about 1 dollar.
Interest is a slice of what you already have. Small savings pay small interest, however good the rate sounds.
problems.useAgain: when a rate per hundred is offered and you want to know whether the payout is worth planning around.
hints: Turn the 3 dollars per 100 into cents per dollar before you look at the 40 at all.
Then ask how many of those cents 40 dollars collects.
problems.socraticHint: How much would have to sit in that account before this rate paid for something you actually want?

variant.prompt: Suppose 300 dollars sits in an account paying about 4 dollars a year for every 100 dollars. About how much does it pay in a year?

problem.prompt: A price sign is a rectangle 12 cm wide and 8 cm tall. Somebody cuts one corner off in a straight line: the cut starts 5 cm along the top edge from the top left corner, and ends 4 cm down the left edge. What is the area of the piece that is left, in square cm?
explanation: The whole sign starts as 12 times 8, which is 96 square cm.
The corner that leaves is a right angled triangle with short sides of 5 cm and 4 cm. Half of 5 times 4 is 10 square cm.
96 take away 10 leaves 86 square cm.
Chopping the leftover piece into a rectangle and a triangle and adding gets the same answer with more sums.
problem.useAgain: when a shape is a plain rectangle with one straight piece cut away.
hints: Draw it on graph paper and draw the cut corner back in with a dotted line.
Work out the whole rectangle first, then work out the piece that left.
problem.socraticHint: Is it fewer sums to add up the piece that is still there, or to take away the piece that went?

variant.prompt: A sign is a rectangle 10 cm wide and 9 cm tall, with a corner cut off in a straight line that runs from 6 cm along the top edge to 3 cm down the left edge. What is the area of the piece left, in square cm?

steps.title: Percent in the shop's mirror: change, margin, interest and the cost of a yes

problems.prompt:
Noor worked out a price change like this: a price fell from 8.00 dollars to 6.00 dollars.
Line 1: The price fell by 2.00 dollars, since 8.00 minus 6.00 is 2.00.
Line 2: A percent fall is measured against where it started, so compare 2.00 with 8.00.
Line 3: One percent of 8.00 is 0.08, and 2.00 is twenty-five of those.
Line 4: So the price fell by 20 percent.
Which line is wrong?
explanation: Line 4 is wrong: line 3 already found 25 lots of one percent, so the fall is 25 percent, not 20.
Lines 1 to 3 are correct: the price fell by 2.00, measured against the starting 8.00, and one percent of 8.00 is 0.08.
The slip is not carrying that 25 through to the final sentence.
Whatever count line 3 finds is the percent, so losing it at the end wastes the whole calculation.
problems.useAgain: when you check a percent change, since the final line's percent has to match the count the working already found.
hints: A percent change compares the change with the starting price, and the percent named at the end must match the counting done just before it.
Compute the percent fall yourself, measured from the original price, and compare it with each line's claim.
problems.socraticHint: Which price is the change measured against, and does the percent named at the end match the count made just before it?

variant.prompt:
Noor worked out another price change: a price fell from 10.00 dollars to 8.00 dollars.
Line 1: The price fell by 2.00 dollars, since 10.00 minus 8.00 is 2.00.
Line 2: A percent fall is measured against where it started, so compare 2.00 with 8.00.
Line 3: One percent of 8.00 is 0.08, and 2.00 is twenty-five of those.
Line 4: This working reaches 25 percent as its final count.
Which line is wrong?

problems.prompt: Suppose you raise a tag from 4.00 dollars to 4.60 dollars. By what percent did the price go up?
explanation: The rise is 4.60 take away 4.00, which is 0.60.
The price grew from 4.00, so that is what the rise gets compared with.
One percent of 4.00 is 4 cents, and 60 cents holds fifteen lots of 4 cents.
So the tag went up by 15 percent.
problems.useAgain: when a price moves up and you want the move as a percent rather than in cents.
hints: Work out how many cents the tag went up by before anything else.
One percent of the old price is a small easy number here; find it, then count how many of them the rise holds.
problems.socraticHint: If the tag had started at 6.00 and gone up the same 60 cents, would the percent be bigger or smaller?

variant.prompt: Suppose a tag goes from 5.00 dollars to 5.40 dollars. By what percent did it go up?

problems.prompt: Suppose a unit sells for 5.00 dollars and costs 3.50 dollars to make. What is the profit on one unit as a percent of its price?
explanation: Profit on one unit is 5.00 take away 3.50, which is 1.50.
Margin asks what slice of the price that profit is, so hold 1.50 against 5.00.
One percent of 5.00 is 5 cents, and 1.50 is thirty of those, so the margin is 30 percent.
Margin as a percent lets your stand and a supermarket be judged on the same scale, because each is measured against its own price.
problems.useAgain: when you want to compare how much your shop keeps with how much a completely different shop keeps.
hints: Work out the profit on one unit before you go anywhere near percents.
Then ask what part of the 5.00 price that profit is, not what part of the 3.50 cost.
problems.socraticHint: Should the profit be held up against the price or against the cost, and what changes if you swap them?

variant.prompt: Suppose a unit sells for 4.00 dollars and costs 3.00 dollars to make. What is the profit as a percent of the price?

problems.prompt: Suppose your stand takes 24 dollars and keeps 6 dollars of profit. A supermarket takes 40,000 dollars in a day and keeps 800. Which one keeps a bigger slice of every dollar it takes?
options: The supermarket, because 800 dollars is far more money than 6 dollars
They keep the same slice, since both numbers are profits
The stand, because it keeps 25 cents of every dollar against the supermarket's 2 cents
There is no fair way to compare a stand with a supermarket
explanation: The two profits cannot be compared as they stand, because the takings behind them are worlds apart.
Turn each into a slice of its own takings. 6 out of 24 is a quarter, which is 25 percent.
800 out of 40,000 is 2 out of every 100, which is 2 percent.
So the stand keeps the bigger slice. Keeping a bigger slice and making more money are different questions, and the supermarket wins the second one easily.
problems.useAgain: when two shops of wildly different sizes have to be judged against each other.
hints: Comparing 6 with 800 answers a question nobody asked here.
Work out what each shop keeps out of every dollar it takes, then compare those two numbers.
problems.socraticHint: Which of these two would you rather own, and is that the same question as which one keeps more of every dollar?

variant.prompt: Suppose your stand takes 30 dollars and keeps 9 dollars. A bakery takes 900 dollars and keeps 90. Which keeps a bigger slice of every dollar?
options: The bakery, because 90 dollars is more money than 9 dollars
The stand, because it keeps 30 cents of every dollar against the bakery's 10 cents
They come out the same once you compare them fairly
The bakery, because it keeps 10 cents of every dollar against the stand's 30 cents

problems.prompt: Suppose you save 30.00 dollars of profit in an account paying 5 percent simple interest a year. How much interest is that in two years, in dollars?
explanation: Simple interest is paid on the 30.00 you put in, year after year, and never on the interest itself.
5 percent is 5 dollars for every 100, so 30.00 earns 1.50 in a year.
Two years at 1.50 is 3.00 dollars.
The family bank last season paid on the new total each year. That is compound interest, and it would have paid a few cents more.
problems.useAgain: when money sits still for a few years and the interest is paid only on what you first put in.
hints: Work out one single year of interest before you think about the second.
5 percent means 5 dollars in every 100, so work out what that is for every 10 dollars first.
problems.socraticHint: What would change about your answer if the account paid interest on the interest as well?

variant.prompt: Suppose 50.00 dollars sits at 4 percent simple interest for three years. How much interest is that, in dollars?

problems.prompt: Suppose the stand took 96.00 dollars in cash. Every cost of the shop came to 30.00 dollars, and all of it was paid with the 30.00 dollars your family lent you at the start. You repay the loan in full out of the cash box. How much is left in the box, in dollars?
explanation: The box holds the 96.00 the stand took.
Borrowed money goes back before anything is called profit, so 30.00 leaves the box first.
96.00 take away 30.00 leaves 66.00.
Do not take the costs off as well. The borrowed 30.00 is what paid them, so removing it once removes them once.
problems.useAgain: when part of the money you started with was borrowed and you are working out what is actually yours.
hints: Ask what the 30.00 of costs was actually paid with, before you subtract anything.
Follow the borrowed 30.00 through the story: where it came from, what it bought, and where it goes back to.
problems.socraticHint: If you subtract the costs and the loan, how many times has that same 30.00 been taken away?

variant.prompt: Suppose a stand took 84.00 dollars, every cost came to 25.00 dollars, and all of it was paid with a 25.00 dollar loan that is now repaid in full from the box. How much is left in the box, in dollars?

problems.prompt: Suppose the shop's profit came to 66.00 dollars and you spent 15 hours of your own time on it. What is the profit for one hour of your time, in dollars?
explanation: Profit for one hour means sharing the whole profit between the hours.
15 lots of 4.00 is 60.00, which leaves 6.00 still to share.
6.00 shared between 15 hours is 40 cents each, so an hour earned 4.40.
This is the number that lets a spring of shop work be compared with anything else those hours could have held.
problems.useAgain: when you want to know what an hour of your own work was worth, not just what the whole job paid.
hints: The question wants one hour's worth, so the profit has to be shared between the hours.
Try 4.00 an hour first and see how much of the 66.00 is still unshared.
problems.socraticHint: Fifteen of your answer have to add back to a number already in the question. Which one?

variant.prompt: Suppose the profit came to 72.00 dollars over 16 hours of your own time. What is the profit for one hour, in dollars?

problems.prompt: Suppose your 66.00 dollars of profit could sit in an account for a year at 5 percent simple interest, or go straight into a second production run. You choose the run. In dollars, what did that yes cost you?
explanation: The cost of a choice is the best thing you gave up to make it.
What is given up here is a year of interest on 66.00 dollars.
5 percent is 5 in every 100, so the year would have paid 3.30.
The run may well earn far more than 3.30. Worth it and free are not the same thing.
problems.useAgain: when you pick one thing and want to name honestly what picking it cost you.
hints: The money you spend is not the answer here. Look at what the other choice would have handed you.
Work out one year of interest on the 66.00 as if you had chosen to save it.
problems.socraticHint: If the second run earns 40.00 dollars, does that make the cost of choosing it nothing?

variant.prompt: Suppose 80.00 dollars of profit could sit for a year at 4 percent simple interest, or buy materials for a bigger second run. You choose the run. In dollars, what did the yes cost you?

steps.title: Flipped across a line, and the bag that remembers nothing

problems.prompt: Point (2, 5) is reflected across the line y = x. What are its new coordinates?
explanation: Reflecting across the line y = x always swaps a point's two coordinates.
So (2, 5) becomes (5, 2).
The mirror line itself is untouched, since every point on it already has equal coordinates.
problems.useAgain: when a point reflects across the line y = x, since that mirror always swaps a point's x and y.
hints: What is special about every point that sits exactly on the line y = x?
Reflecting across that line swaps the two coordinates.
problems.socraticHint: If a point already had equal x and y, would reflecting it across y = x move it at all?

variant.prompt: Point (-3, 4) is reflected across the line y = x. What are its new coordinates?

problems.prompt: Point (1, 4) is reflected across the vertical line x = 3. What are its new coordinates?
explanation: The point sits 2 units left of the mirror line x = 3, since 3 minus 1 is 2.
The reflection lands 2 units on the other side of the mirror: 3 plus 2 is 5.
The y-coordinate never changes in a reflection across a vertical line, so it stays 4.
problems.useAgain: when a point reflects across a vertical line that is not the y-axis, by measuring its distance from the mirror on each side.
hints: How far is the point from the mirror line, and on which side?
The reflection sits that same distance on the other side of the mirror; the y-coordinate does not change.
problems.socraticHint: Does reflecting across a vertical line ever change how high or low a point sits?

variant.prompt: Point (7, 2) is reflected across the vertical line x = 3. What are its new coordinates?

problems.prompt: A bag has 3 blue marbles and 2 green marbles, 5 total. You draw one, note its color, put it back, then draw again. What is the probability, as a fraction, both draws are blue?
explanation: Putting the marble back means the bag is identical for both draws.
Each draw is blue with probability 3/5.
problems.useAgain: when a marble is drawn, replaced, then drawn again, so the two draws are independent and their chances multiply.
hints: Does replacing the marble change the chances for the second draw?
Multiply the chance of blue by itself, once for each draw.
problems.socraticHint: If the bag looks exactly the same for both draws, are the two draws independent of each other?

variant.prompt: A bag has 4 blue marbles and 1 green marble, 5 total. You draw one, put it back, then draw again. What is the probability, as a fraction, both draws are blue?

problems.prompt: Using the same bag, 3 blue and 2 green out of 5, replaced each time, what is the probability of drawing green then blue, in that exact order, as a fraction?
explanation: The order matters here, so multiply the chances in the order they are asked for.
Green first is 2/5, then blue is 3/5.
problems.useAgain: when a probability question asks for one exact order of results, not just any combination.
hints: Write the chance for the first draw and the chance for the second draw separately, in the order asked.
Multiply those two chances together.
problems.socraticHint: Does asking for green then blue mean the same thing as asking for one green and one blue in either order?

variant.prompt: Using a bag with 4 blue and 1 green out of 5, replaced each time, what is the probability of drawing green then blue, in that exact order, as a fraction?

steps.title: Three geometry peaks: angles that add up, areas in pieces, and the square on the side

problems.prompt: Three angles sit side by side along a straight line. Two of them are 47 degrees and 68 degrees. How big is the third, in degrees?
explanation: Angles sitting in a row along a straight line always hold 180 degrees between them.
47 and 68 make 115.
180 take away 115 leaves 65 degrees.
problems.useAgain: when angles sit in a row along a straight edge and one of them is missing.
hints: A straight line is worth a fixed number of degrees, however many angles it is cut into.
Add the two angles you know before you do anything else.
problems.socraticHint: What happens to the third angle if the other two both grow a little?

variant.prompt: Two angles along a straight line are 52 degrees and 39 degrees, with one more beside them filling the line. How big is that third angle, in degrees?

problems.prompt: A triangle has a 90 degree corner and a 34 degree corner. One side is extended straight past the third corner, making an angle outside the triangle there. How big is that outside angle, in degrees?
explanation: The three corners of a triangle hold 180 degrees between them. So the third corner is 180 take away 90 take away 34, which is 56.
The extended side makes a straight line at that corner, and a straight line holds 180 degrees.
180 take away 56 is 124 degrees.
Notice 90 plus 34 is 124 as well. An outside angle always matches the two corners it does not touch.
problems.useAgain: when a side of a triangle is extended and the angle spilling outside it is what you need.
hints: Find the third corner of the triangle first; the outside angle is standing right next to it.
That corner and the outside angle together lie along one straight line.
problems.socraticHint: Try it again with two corners of your own choosing. Does the outside angle keep matching the same two corners?

variant.prompt: A triangle has a 100 degree corner and a 25 degree corner, and a side is extended straight past the third corner. How big is the angle outside the triangle there, in degrees?

problems.prompt: In an isosceles triangle the two equal sides meet at a 40 degree corner. How big is each of the two equal corners at the base?
explanation: All three corners hold 180 degrees, and the 40 degree corner has taken some of it.
180 take away 40 leaves 140 degrees to be shared out.
The two base corners are equal, so each one takes half of 140, which is 70 degrees.
140 is the trap. It is the pair of them together, not one of them.
problems.useAgain: when a triangle has two sides the same length and only one of its angles is given.
hints: Take the corner you know away from the triangle's total first.
What is left belongs to two corners that are the same size as each other.
problems.socraticHint: Which two of the three corners have to be equal here, and what tells you so?

variant.prompt: In an isosceles triangle the two equal sides meet at a 96 degree corner. How big is each of the two equal base corners?

problems.prompt: A table top is an L shape. It would be a 90 cm by 60 cm rectangle, except that a 40 cm by 25 cm rectangle is missing from one corner. What is the area of the table top, in square cm?
explanation: Start with the whole rectangle: 90 times 60 is 5400 square cm.
The missing corner is 40 times 25, which is 1000 square cm.
5400 take away 1000 is 4400 square cm.
Chopping the L into two rectangles and adding them lands in the same place, with more sums.
problems.useAgain: when a shape is a rectangle with a rectangular bite taken out of it.
hints: Draw it, and draw the missing corner back in with a dotted line.
Work out the area of the full rectangle first, then the area of the piece that is not there.
problems.socraticHint: Is it fewer sums to add up the pieces that are there, or to take away the piece that is not?

variant.prompt: A board would be an 80 cm by 50 cm rectangle, except a 30 cm by 20 cm rectangle is missing from one corner. What is its area, in square cm?

problems.prompt: A rectangle is 10 cm across and 6 cm tall. A dot is marked somewhere on the top edge, anywhere at all, and lines are drawn from the dot to the two bottom corners. What is the area of that triangle, in square cm?
explanation: The triangle stands on the whole bottom edge, so its base is 10 cm.
Its top point sits on the top edge, so its height is the 6 cm between the two edges, wherever the dot slides to.
Half of 10 times 6 is 30 square cm.
Moving the dot changes the shape and never the area, which is why the question is allowed to leave it anywhere.
problems.useAgain: when a triangle sits inside a rectangle with a whole side of it as the base.
hints: Draw it twice, once with the dot near a corner and once with it in the middle, and compare the two.
Name the triangle's base and its height before you reach for any rule.
problems.socraticHint: What happens to the two leftover pieces of the rectangle as the dot slides along the top edge?

variant.prompt: A rectangle is 14 cm across and 5 cm tall, with a dot anywhere on the top edge joined to the two bottom corners. What is the area of the triangle, in square cm?

problems.prompt: A right angled triangle has the two sides that meet at the right angle measuring 9 cm and 12 cm. How long is the longest side, in cm?
explanation: Square the two short sides: 9 times 9 is 81, and 12 times 12 is 144.
The two small squares exactly fill the square on the longest side, so that square holds 225.
225 is 15 times 15, so the longest side is 15 cm.
9, 12, 15 is 3, 4, 5 with every side tripled, which is why it comes out whole.
problems.useAgain: when two sides of a right angled triangle are known and the third one is not.
hints: Draw a square outwards from each of the two short sides and work out how many square cm each one holds.
Add those two areas, then ask what number multiplied by itself makes the total.
problems.socraticHint: Do these two lengths remind you of a smaller triangle you already know by heart?

variant.prompt: The two sides meeting at the right angle are 8 cm and 15 cm. How long is the longest side, in cm?

problems.prompt: A triangle has sides of 5 cm, 12 cm and 14 cm. Somebody says it must be right angled. True or false?
explanation: Test it rather than trusting it. The squares on the two shorter sides have to fill the square on the longest exactly.
5 times 5 is 25 and 12 times 12 is 144, so together they hold 169.
The square on 14 holds 196, and 169 is not 196, so there is no right angle.
It is imitating 5, 12, 13, which is a real triple. One centimetre is enough to break it.
problems.useAgain: when three side lengths are given and the question is whether the right angle is really there.
hints: The longest side is the one the other two get held up against.
Work out the two smaller squares and add them before you look at the biggest one.
problems.socraticHint: If the squares on the two shorter sides were to fill the square on the longest side exactly, how long would that longest side be?

variant.prompt: A triangle has sides of 7 cm, 24 cm and 25 cm. Somebody says it must be right angled. True or false?

problems.prompt: A stretch peak, untimed. A right triangle has one leg of length 41 and a whole-number hypotenuse. What is the only possible hypotenuse greater than 41?
explanation: Pythagoras says the hypotenuse c and the other leg n satisfy c squared minus n squared equals 41 squared, since one leg is 41.
Factor the left side: (c minus n)(c plus n) equals 41 squared, which is 1,681.
41 is prime, so 1,681 only splits into 1 times itself: c minus n is 1 and c plus n is 1,681.
Adding those two: 2c is 1,682, so c is 841, which makes the word only in the prompt a checkable claim rather than a guess.
problems.useAgain: when a right triangle's hypotenuse has to be a whole number and one leg is prime, since the difference of squares only splits one way.
hints: Write c squared minus n squared as a product of two factors before you try any numbers.
A prime squared has only one way to split into two whole-number factors greater than zero: 1 and itself.
problems.socraticHint: If 41 were not prime, would c squared minus n squared still split into only one pair of factors?

variant.prompt: A right triangle has one leg of length 101 and a whole-number hypotenuse. What is the only possible hypotenuse greater than 101?

steps.title: Explain it in writing: margin, and the fair comparison
steps.prompt: Take one real unit off your own tags: what it sells for, and what it costs you to make. Write the profit on that one unit, then write that profit as a percent of its price, showing every step rather than the answer alone. Then do the same sum for a shop that takes 40,000 dollars and keeps 800. Finish with three sentences: which number is bigger, which shop keeps the bigger slice of every dollar, and why those two questions have different answers.

steps.title: Explain it out loud
steps.prompt: Draw the sliding dot peak on graph paper with the camera watching: the rectangle, then the triangle three times over with the dot in three different places, shading each one. Then say the three lines that finish it: what the triangle's base is, what its height is, and why the area refuses to change when the dot moves. Close by saying how many positions of the dot you had to check.
